entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.65.1-Ps.65.4">Psa 65:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9639" type="x-p"/> The praise of God on account of the mercy with which He rules out of Zion. The lxx renders σοὶ πρέπει ὕμνος, but דּומיּה, <hi type="italic">tibi par est, h. e. convenit laus</hi> (Ewald), is not a usage of the language (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.33.1">Psa 33:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.7">Jer 10:7</reference>). דּמיּה signifies, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.22.3">Psa 22:3</reference>, silence, and as an ethical notion, resignation, Psa 62:2. According to the position of the words it looks like the subject, and תּהלּה like the predicate. The accents at least (<hi type="italic">Illuj, Shalsheleth</hi>) assume the relationship of the one word to the other to be that of predicate and subject; consequently it is not: To Thee belongeth resignation, praise (Hengstenberg), but: To Thee is resignation praise, i.e., resignation is (given or presented) to Thee as praise. Hitzig obtains the same meaning by an alteration of the text: לך דמיה תהלּל; but opposed to this is the fact that הלּל ל is not found anywhere in the Psalter, but only in the writings of the chronicler. And since it is clear that the words לך תהלה belong together (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.4">Psa 40:4</reference>), the poet had no need to fear any ambiguity when he inserted dmyh between them as that which is given to God as praise in Zion. What is intended is that submission or resignation to God which gives up its cause to God and allows Him to act on its behalf, renouncing all impatient meddling and interference (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.14">Exo 14:14</reference>). The second member of the sentence affirms that this praise of pious resignation does not remain unanswered. Just as God in Zion is praised by prayer which resigns our own will silently to His, so also to Him are vows paid when He fulfils such prayer. That the answers to prayer are evidently thought of in connection with this, we see from <reference osisRef="Ps.65.3">Psa 65:3</reference>, where God is addressed as the “Hearer or Answerer of prayer.” To Him as being the Hearer and Answerer of prayer all flesh comes, and in fact, as עדיך implies (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.45.24">Isa 45:24</reference>), without finding help anywhere else, it clear a way for itself until it gets to Him; i.e., men, absolutely dependent, impotent in themselves and helpless, both collectively and individually (those only excepted who are determined to perish or despair), flee to Him as their final refuge and help. Before all else it is the prayer for the forgiveness of sin which He graciously answers. The perfect in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">Psa 65:4</reference></hi> is followed by the future in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.65.4">Psa 65:4</reference></hi>. The former, in accordance with the sense, forms a hypothetical protasis: granted that the instances of faults have been too powerful for me, i.e., (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.4.13">Gen 4:13</reference>) an intolerable burden to me, our transgressions are expiated by Thee (who alone canst and also art willing to do it). דּברי is not less significant than in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.20">Psa 35:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.27">Psa 105:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.145.5">Psa 145:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.2">1Sa 10:2</reference>; 2Sa 11:18.: it separates the general fact into its separate instances and circumstances. How blessed therefore is the lot of that man whom (supply אשׁר) God chooses and brings near, i.e., removes into His vicinity, that he may inhabit His courts (future with the force of a clause expressing a purpose, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Job.30.28">Job 30:28</reference>, which see), i.e., that there, where He sits enthroned and reveals Himself, he may have his true home and be as if at home (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.15.1">Psa 15:1</reference>)! The congregation gathered around Zion is esteemed worthy of this distinction among the nations of the earth; it therefore encourages itself in the blessed consciousness of this its privilege flowing from free grace (בחר), to enjoy in full draughts (שּבע with בּ as in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference>) the abundant goodness or blessing (טוּב) of God’s house, of the holy (ἅγιον) of His temple, i.e., of His holy temple (קדשׁ as in <reference osisRef="Ps.46.5">Psa 46:5</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.57.15">Isa 57:15</reference>). For for all that God’s grace offers us we can give Him no better thanks than to hunger and thirst after it, and satisfy our poor soul therewith.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.65.5-Ps.65.8">Psa 65:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen9639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9640" type="x-p"/> The praise of God on account of the lovingkindness which Israel as a people among the peoples has experienced. The future תּעננוּ confesses, as a present, a fact of experience that still holds good in all times to come. נוראות might, according to <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">Psa 139:14</reference>, be an accusative of the more exact definition; but why not, according to <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.10">1Sa 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.9.3">Job 9:3</reference>, a second accusative under the government of the verb? God answers the prayer of His people superabundantly. He replies to it גוראות, terrible deeds, viz., בּצדק, by a rule which stringently executes the will of His righteousness (vid., on <reference osisRef="Jer.42.6">Jer 42:6</reference>); in this instance against the oppressors of His people, so that henceforth everywhere upon earth He is a ground of confidence to all those who are oppressed. “The sea (ים construct state, as is frequently the case, with the retention of the <hi type="italic">å</hi>) of the distant ones” is that of the regions lying afar off (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1">Psa 56:1</reference>). Venema observes, <hi type="italic">Significatur, Deum esse certissimum praesidium, sive agnoscatur ab hominibus et ei fidatur, sive non</hi> (therefore similar to γνόντες, <reference osisRef="Rom.1.21">Rom 1:21</reference>; <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. S. 347; tr. p. 408). But according tot he connection and the subjective colouring the idea seems to have, מבטח וגו is to be understood of the believing acknowledgment which the God of Israel attains among all mankind by reason of His judicial and redemptive self-attestation (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.33.13">Isa 33:13</reference>; 2Ch 32:22.). In the natural world and among men He proves Himself to be the Being girded with power to whom everything must yield. He it is who setteth fast the mountains (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.10.12">Jer 10:12</reference>) and stilleth the raging of the ocean. In connection with the giant mountains the poet may have had even the worldly powers (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.41.15">Isa 41:15</reference>) in his mind; in connection with the seas he gives expression to this allegorical conjunction of thoughts. The roaring of the billows and the wild tumult of the nations as a mass in the empire of the world, both are stilled by the threatening of the God of Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.17.12-Isa.17.14">Isa 17:12-14</reference>). When He shall overthrow the proud empire of the world, whose tyranny the earth has been made to feel far and wide, then will reverential fear of Him and exultant joy at the end of the thraldom (vid., <reference osisRef="Isa.13.4-Isa.13.8">Isa 13:4-8</reference>) become universal. אותת (from the originally feminine אות = <hi type="italic">ăwăjat</hi>, from אוה, to mark, Num 34:10), σημεῖα, is the name given here to His marvellous interpositions in the history of our earth. קצוי, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.6">Psa 65:6</reference> (also in <reference osisRef="Isa.26.15">Isa 26:15</reference>), out of construction is קצות. “The exit places of the morning and of the evening” are the East and West with reference to those who dwell there. Luther erroneously understands מוצאי as directly referring to the creatures which at morning and evening “sport about (<hi type="italic">webern</hi>), i.e., go safely and joyfully out and in.” The meaning is, the regions whence the morning breaks forth and where the evening sets. The construction is zeugmatic so far as בּוא, not יצא, is said of the evening sun, but only to a certain extent, for neither does one say נבוא ערב (Ewald). Perret-Gentil renders it correctly: <hi type="italic">les lieux d'où surgissent l'aube et le crepuscule</hi>. God makes both these to shout for joy, inasmuch as He commands a calm to the din of war.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.65.9-Ps.65.13">Psa 65:9-13</reference> <div eID="gen9640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9641" type="x-p"/> The praise of God on account of the present year’s rich blessing, which He has bestowed upon the land of His people. In <reference osisRef="Ps.65.10">Psa 65:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.11">Psa 65:11</reference> God is thanked for having sent down the rain required for the ploughing (vid., <hi type="italic">Commentary on Isaiah</hi>, ii. 522) and for the increase of the seed sown, so that, as vv. 12-14 affirm, there is the prospect of a rich harvest. The harvest itself, as follows from v. 14 <hi type="italic">b</hi>, is not yet housed. The whole of <reference osisRef="Ps.65.10">Psa 65:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.11">Psa 65:11</reference> is a retrospect; in vv. 12-14 the whole is a description of the blessing standing before their eyes, which God has put upon the year now drawing to a close. Certainly, if the forms רוּה and נחת were supplicatory imperatives, then the prayer for the early or seed-time rain would attach itself to the retrospect in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.11">Psa 65:11</reference>, and the standpoint would be not about the time of the Passover and Pentecost, both festivals belonging to the beginning of the harvest, but about the time of the feast of Tabernacles, the festival of thanksgiving for the harvest, and vv. 12-14 would be a glance into the future (Hitzig). But there is nothing to indicate that in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.11">Psa 65:11</reference> the retrospect changes into a looking forward. The poet goes on with the same theme, and also arranges the words accordingly, for which reason רוּה and נחת are not to be understood in any other way. שׁקק beside העשׁיר (to enrich) signifies to cause to run over, overflow, i.e., to put anything in a state of plenty or abundance, from שׁוּק (<hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. <reference osisRef="Joel.2.24">Joe 2:24</reference>, to yield in abundance), Arab, <hi type="italic">sâq</hi>, to push, impel, to cause to go on in succession and to follow in succession. רבּת (for which we find רבּה in <reference osisRef="Ps.62.3">Psa 62:3</reference>) is an adverb, copiously, richly (<reference osisRef="Ps.120.6">Psa 120:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Psa 123:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1">Psa 129:1</reference>), like מאת, a hundred times (<reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ecc 8:12</reference>). תּעשׁרנּה is <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. with the middle syllable shortened, Ges. §53, 3, rem. 4. The fountain (פּלג) of God is the name given here to His inexhaustible stores of blessing, and more particularly the fulness of the waters of the heavens from which He showers down fertilizing rain. כּן, “thus thoroughly,” forms an alliteration with הכין, to prepare, and thereby receives a peculiar twofold colouring. The meaning is: God, by raising and tending, prepared the produce of the field which the inhabitants of the land needed; for He thus thoroughly prepared the land in conformity with the fulness of His fountain, viz., by copiously watering (רוּה <hi type="italic">infin. absol</hi>. instead of רוּה, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.12">1Sa 3:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.10">2Ch 24:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.22.22">Exo 22:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">Jer 14:19</reference>; Hos 6:9) the furrows of the land and pressing down, i.e., softening by means of rain, its ridges (גּדוּדה, defective plural, as e.g., in Rth 2:13), which the ploughshare has made. תּלם (related by root with Arab. <hi type="italic">tll , tell</hi>, a hill, prop. that which is thrown out to a place, that which is thrown up, a mound) signifies a furrow as being formed by casting up or (if from Arab. <hi type="italic">ṯlm , ébrécher</hi>, to make a fracture, rent, or notch in anything) by tearing into, breaking up the ground; גּדוּד (related by root with <hi type="italic">uchdûd</hi> and <hi type="italic">chaṭṭ</hi>, the usual Arabic words for a furrow<note placement="foot">Fürst erroneously explains תּלם as a bed or strip of ground between two deep furrows, in distinction from מענה or מענית (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>), a furrow. Beds such as we have in our potato fields are unknown to Syrian agriculture. There is a mode which may be approximately compared with it called <hi type="italic">ketif</hi> (כּתף), another far wider called <hi type="italic">meskeba</hi> (משׂכּבה). The Arabic <hi type="italic">tilm</hi> (תּלם, Hebrew תּלם = <hi type="italic">talm</hi>), according to the Kamûs (as actually in Magrebinish Arabic) <hi type="italic">talam</hi> (תּלם), corresponds exact to our furrow, i.e., (as the Turkish Kamûs explains) a ditch-like fissure which the iron of the plough cuts into the field. entries.content_plain: Psa 65:9-13 The praise of God on account of the present year’s rich blessing, which He has bestowed upon the land of His people. In Psa 65:10 , Psa 65:11 God is thanked for having sent down the rain required for the ploughing (vid., Commentary on Isaiah , ii. 522) and for the increase of the seed sown, so that, as vv. 12-14 affirm, there is the prospect of a rich harvest. The harvest itself, as follows from v. 14 b , is not yet housed. The whole of Psa 65:10 , Psa 65:11 is a retrospect; in vv. 12-14 the whole is a description of the blessing standing before their eyes, which God has put upon the year now drawing to a close. Certainly, if the forms רוּה and נחת were supplicatory imperatives, then the prayer for the early or seed-time rain would attach itself to the retrospect in Psa 65:11 , and the standpoint would be not about the time of the Passover and Pentecost, both festivals belonging to the beginning of the harvest, but about the time of the feast of Tabernacles, the festival of thanksgiving for the harvest, and vv. 12-14 would be a glance into the future (Hitzig). But there is nothing to indicate that in Psa 65:11 the retrospect changes into a looking forward. The poet goes on with the same theme, and also arranges the words accordingly, for which reason רוּה and נחת are not to be understood in any other way. שׁקק beside העשׁיר (to enrich) signifies to cause to run over, overflow, i.e., to put anything in a state of plenty or abundance, from שׁוּק ( Hiph . Joe 2:24 , to yield in abundance), Arab, sâq , to push, impel, to cause to go on in succession and to follow in succession. רבּת (for which we find רבּה in Psa 62:3 ) is an adverb, copiously, richly ( Psa 120:6 ; Psa 123:4 ; Psa 129:1 ), like מאת, a hundred times ( Ecc 8:12 ). תּעשׁרנּה is Hiph . with the middle syllable shortened, Ges. §53, 3, rem. 4. The fountain (פּלג) of God is the name given here to His inexhaustible stores of blessing, and more particularly the fulness of the waters of the heavens from which He showers down fertilizing rain. כּן, “thus thoroughly,” forms an alliteration with הכין, to prepare, and thereby receives a peculiar twofold colouring. The meaning is: God, by raising and tending, prepared the produce of the field which the inhabitants of the land needed; for He thus thoroughly prepared the land in conformity with the fulness of His fountain, viz., by copiously watering (רוּה infin. absol . instead of רוּה, as in 1Sa 3:12 ; 2Ch 24:10 ; Exo 22:22 ; Jer 14:19 ; Hos 6:9) the furrows of the land and pressing down, i.e., softening by means of rain, its ridges (גּדוּדה, defective plural, as e.g., in Rth 2:13), which the ploughshare has made. תּלם (related by root with Arab. tll , tell , a hill, prop. that which is thrown out to a place, that which is thrown up, a mound) signifies a furrow as being formed by casting up or (if from Arab. ṯlm , ébrécher , to make a fracture, rent, or notch in anything) by tearing into, breaking up the ground; גּדוּד (related by root with uchdûd and chaṭṭ , the usual Arabic words for a furrow Fürst erroneously explains תּלם as a bed or strip of ground between two deep furrows, in distinction from מענה or מענית (vid., on Psa 129:3 ), a furrow. Beds such as we have in our potato fields are unknown to Syrian agriculture. There is a mode which may be approximately compared with it called ketif (כּתף), another far wider called meskeba (משׂכּבה). Neshwân (i. 491) says: “The verb talam , fut. jatlum and jatlim , signifies in Jemen and in the Ghôr (the land on the shore of the Red Sea) the crevices (Arab. 'l - šuqûq ) which the ploughman forms, and tilm , collective plural tilâm , is, in the countries mentioned, a furrow of the corn-field. Some persons pronounce the word even thilm , collective plural thilâm .” Thus it is at the present day universally in Ḥaurân ; in Edre‛ât I heard the water-furrow of a corn-field called thilm el - kanâh (Arab. ṯlm 'l - qnât ). But this pronunciation with Arab. ṯ is certainly not the original one, but has arisen through a substitution of the cognate and more familiar verbal stem Arab. ṯlm , cf. šrm , to slit ( shurêm , a harelip). In other parts of Syria and Palestine, also where the distinction between the sounds Arab. t and ṯ is carefully observed, I have only heard the pronunciation tilm . - Wetzstein.) as being formed by cutting into the ground. In Psa 65:12 the year in itself appears as a year of divine goodness (טובה, bonitas ), and the prospective blessing of harvest as the crown which is set upon it.
